summary: Discusses a proposed extension to the Internet architecture to provide integrated services, supporting real-time as well as non-real-time traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some data, like a phone call, cannot wait. This describes how the Internet could give urgent traffic a fast lane.

subtitle: The architecture that proposed adding guaranteed and predictive real-time service, and link sharing, to best-effort IP.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications such as voice and video often work poorly across the Internet because of variable queueing delays and congestion losses, and IP offers only best-effort delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes an integrated services model with guaranteed and predictive real-time service plus controlled link sharing, realised by a packet scheduler, classifier, admission control and a reservation setup protocol (RSVP).
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational overview that argues it is time to begin the engineering needed before deployment. It leaves policy, authentication and several mechanisms for further study.

today: RFC 1633 is an Informational overview. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo itself calls for further engineering before deployment.

sections.title: The Problem: Real-Time Traffic on a Best-Effort Net
sections.content:
Multicasts of IETF meetings across the Internet were a large experiment in sending digitized voice and video over a packet-switched network. They showed that real-time applications often do not work well because of variable queueing delays and congestion losses. The Internet as originally conceived offers only a very simple quality of service (QoS): point-to-point best-effort delivery.

The memo adds a second goal. Network operators want to divide traffic into administrative classes and give each a minimum percentage of a link under overload, while unused bandwidth stays available. This is called controlled link-sharing. The memo uses the term integrated services (IS) for a service model that includes best-effort service, real-time service and controlled link sharing. The extension must be designed for multicast from the start, since simply generalizing from unicast does not work.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet treats every packet the same, like one long queue. A video call needs its packets on time, so the memo asks for a way to treat different traffic differently.

sections.title: Assumptions and the Reference Framework
sections.content:
The memo rests on several assumptions. Resources such as bandwidth must be explicitly managed, so resource reservation and admission control are key building blocks. It rejects three arguments against reservations: that bandwidth will be infinite, that simple priority is enough, and that applications can adapt. It also assumes one common infrastructure and a single internet-layer protocol for real-time and non-real-time traffic, and one service model for the Internet.

This means routers need flow-specific state, a change from the principle that flow state lives in end systems. A flow is a distinguishable stream of related datagrams that needs the same QoS, and it is simplex: one source, N destinations. The reference framework has four components.

  • Packet scheduler: manages forwarding of packet streams using queues, at the output driver.
  • Classifier: maps each incoming packet into a class that gets the same treatment.
  • Admission control: decides whether a new flow can get the requested QoS without harming earlier guarantees.
  • Reservation setup protocol: creates and maintains flow-specific state in hosts and routers.

An application states its needs with a flowspec, which the setup protocol carries and admission control tests.
sections.plainLanguage: A router would need four helpers: one who sorts packets into groups, one who decides who goes first, one who says yes or no to new requests, and one who passes the requests along.

sections.title: The Integrated Services Model
sections.content:
The core service model deals almost only with time of delivery, so per-packet delay is the central quantity, and the only quantitative commitments are bounds on maximum and minimum delay. The memo separates real-time applications, which need data by a certain time or the data is worthless, from elastic applications, which always wait for data.

For real-time "playback" applications, the receiver buffers data and replays it at a fixed offset delay. Intolerant applications need a perfectly reliable delay bound, so the memo proposes guaranteed service. Tolerant and adaptive applications can accept some late packets, so it proposes predictive service, a fairly reliable but not perfectly reliable bound that is presumably cheaper. Elastic applications get "as-soon-as-possible" service, called best-effort, in several classes and without admission control.

The model adds link-sharing, where aggregate link bandwidth is shared among entities by specified shares, possibly in a hierarchy. It also proposes "preemptable" and "expendable" packets that can be dropped, discusses usage feedback (accounting) as a contentious issue it does not resolve, and describes a simple grant-or-refuse reservation model plus a more complex two-pass model.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic must arrive on time or it is useless, like a live call. Other traffic, like email, just needs to get there. The memo offers a strict promise, a softer promise, and the normal best-effort way.

sections.title: Traffic Control Mechanisms
sections.content:
A router can select a route, then forward, drop, reorder or hold a packet. Packet scheduling reorders the output queue. Strict priority can starve lower classes completely, while round-robin variants such as Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ) can allocate a link into specified shares. Packet dropping matters too: for TCP a drop signals congestion, and for real-time traffic dropping one packet can cut the delay of those behind it. Dropping and scheduling must be coordinated.

Classification needs more than the destination address. The classifier may look at fields such as source address, protocol number and ports, or a "flow-id" field might shortcut the work. Admission control can use worst-case parameters or measured usage; the algorithm in each router is a local matter.

The memo cites a result by Parekh that WFQ plus a characterised traffic source, for example one fitting a token bucket, gives an absolute upper bound on delay. As a proof of concept it describes the CSZ scheme, which uses WFQ for guaranteed flows and link shares, priority between predictive and best-effort service, and FIFO inside predictive sub-classes. The memo stresses that CSZ is not mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can line packets up in different ways: strict VIP lanes, or fair turns for each group. The memo says fair turns are the more flexible choice, and checking the packet's labels tells the router which lane to use.

sections.title: RSVP and Routing
sections.content:
The memo describes requirements for a reservation setup protocol: designed for multicast, able to handle heterogeneous receivers, robust and scalable, and able to support advance reservation. RSVP was designed to meet them. A session is defined by the common IP destination address of the receivers. A reservation request pairs a flowspec (the amount of resources) with a filter spec (which packets receive them).

RSVP offers three reservation styles: wildcard, fixed-filter and dynamic-filter. It is receiver-initiated, which scales for large multicast trees and varied receivers. It uses soft state: reservation state is cached information installed and periodically refreshed by end hosts, and unused state is timed out by routers. If a route changes, refresh messages install state along the new route.

The memo lists four routing issues: finding a route that supports reservation, finding one with enough capacity, adapting to a route failure, and adapting to a route change without failure, for which it suggests "route pinning". RSVP is designed to work with any current routing protocol without modification, which the memo calls a short-term compromise.
sections.plainLanguage: The person receiving the video asks for the fast lane, and every router along the way keeps that promise only as long as the request keeps being renewed, like re-booking a table.

sections.title: Authentication and Policy
sections.content: Resource reservation means some users get privileged service, so policy and administrative controls are needed. That leads to two authentication needs: authentication of users who make reservation requests, and authentication of packets that claim the right to use reserved resources. The memo does not address these issues further and leaves them for study.
sections.plainLanguage: If some people get a fast lane, the network has to check who is allowed to use it. The memo says this still needs to be worked out.

viz.caption: THE FOUR COMPONENTS OF THE REFERENCE FRAMEWORK

items.title: Packet scheduler
items.text: Manages forwarding of packet streams with queues at the output driver.

items.title: Classifier
items.text: Maps each incoming packet into a class.

items.title: Admission control
items.text: Accepts or rejects a new flow at each node.

items.title: Reservation setup protocol
items.text: Creates and maintains flow state in hosts and routers; RSVP.
